e.t: This word means “to grasp” or “to perceive”—to take hold of something with the mind so that its meaning becomes understood. It describes recognizing or comprehending what is being communicated, rather than merely hearing words. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 9:45. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is mental understanding or recognition.

e.t: This word means “fisherman,” referring to a person who catches fish. It is a noun describing people whose work involves fishing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, in passages mentioning fishermen in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The word appears especially in the accounts involving people called from their fishing work to follow Jesus. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a fisherman is someone engaged in catching fish. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about that person in each occurrence.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to leave” or “to withdraw.” It describes moving away from a place, person, or situation, whether departing normally or stepping back for safety or another purpose. The word appears 14 times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense is a recurring description of departure rather than a rare or specialized term. The surrounding passage determines what prompted the leaving in each occurrence.

me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Feminine

e.t: This word means “opposition”: the condition of being set against something else. It identifies a stance, claim, or force that stands over against another, rather than merely describing two things as different. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 1 Timothy 6:20. The precise force of that single occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage for its full sense in context.

Its basic focus is the act of declaring or reporting information rather than keeping it private. The word occurs 45 times in the Greek New Testament, showing regular use for sharing news or conveying what someone has learned or witnessed.

e.t: This word means “to conceal” or “to hide”—to keep something from being seen, known, or understood. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times and describes the withholding or concealment of something, whether information, wisdom, or a revealed purpose. Its basic sense is straightforward, while the surrounding sentence determines what is hidden and from whom. The word occurs in Luke, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, and Colossians, showing its use across both Gospel and apostolic writing.

e.t: This word means “to eat,” with a particular sense of eating an early meal. It describes the act of taking food and may be used for an ordinary meal rather than for a figurative idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Luke and John. Its exact emphasis in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains eating, especially an early meal.

me: Adjective, Accusative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: “Eatable” or “edible” describes something suitable or possible to eat. It functions as an adjective, identifying food or another thing by whether it can be consumed. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Luke 24:41. Its basic meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes there. The word’s lexical sense is limited to the idea of being fit to eat, without requiring additional spiritual or symbolic meaning.

gl: the twin gods Castor and Pollux
d: The Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus and Leda, and patrons of sailors.
me: Noun, Dative, Plural, Masculine, Title

e.t: This word refers to “the twin gods,” specifically “the twin gods Castor and Pollux.” It is a proper name used for the pair known together as the Dioscuri. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 28:11. The word identifies the figures themselves rather than describing a general quality or action. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the reference is being used there.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its basic sense is “seventy times”. It refers to a counted number of repetitions rather than describing a person, object, or action by itself. As a Greek New Testament word, it appears once, in Matthew 18:22. The surrounding verse is needed to understand how this number functions in that statement, but the word itself supplies the numerical measure. It is therefore best understood plainly as expressing seventy repetitions or occurrences.

e.t: This word means “working,” referring to an active work or operation. It describes something being carried out or producing an effect, rather than merely remaining as an ability or possibility. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, both times in 1 Corinthians 12, where its wording is associated with different kinds of activity. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains active working or operation. me: PREPosition

e.t: This word means “beyond,” expressing a position or distance farther than a stated point or boundary. It points to something lying on the other side of, or farther than, what has already been mentioned. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:43. Its basic sense is geographical or positional, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what boundary or point is being exceeded.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “wool,” the natural fiber used as a material. It functions as a straightforward noun naming wool rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 9:19 and Revelation 1:14. Its basic meaning remains the same in both references; the surrounding verse determines how the material contributes to each passage’s description. This word is therefore concrete and specific, referring to wool itself.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, with occurrences in Luke, Titus, James, and 2 Peter. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains pleasure or enjoyment.

e.t: Heli is a personal name referring to an individual named Heli. It functions as a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke 3:23. The available rendering preserves the name as “Heli,” so its ordinary meaning is the person’s name itself; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s specific role in the passage.

d: (properly: to lead one as my prisoner in a triumphal procession, hence) to lead around, make a show (spectacle) of, cause to triumph.

e.t: This word describes triumph—especially the act of leading someone in a triumphal procession. It can express public victory, conquest, or the display of a victor’s success. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Corinthians 2:14 and Colossians 2:15. Its central picture is not merely private happiness, but triumph openly displayed as a victorious leader brings others into the procession. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on triumph itself or on being led in triumph.

e.t: “Jeremiah” is a personal name that identifies someone called Jeremiah. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears three times, all in Matthew. It is used as a person’s name rather than as a description, action, or quality. The name occurs in Matthew 2:17, Matthew 16:14, and Matthew 27:9. Its exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

It occurs 35 times in 34 New Testament verses, referring to more than one individual, including Joseph connected with Jesus’ family and Joseph of Arimathea. The surrounding passage is needed to determine which Joseph is meant in any particular verse.

e.t: This word means “judge” or “judges”—a person or persons who decide matters, assess conduct, or administer justice. It is a noun referring to someone with judicial authority or responsibility. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 19 times across 17 verses, including passages that speak of a judge in legal disputes and of people who judge others. The word can therefore describe an official judge as well as those acting in the role of evaluating or deciding. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: Malchus, a servant of the high-priest at Jerusalem.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Malchus is a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one individual in the Greek New Testament and occurs once, in John 18:10. The English rendering preserves the name as “Malchus,” so its meaning is primarily its role as a personal designation, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about the person being named.

e.t: This word means “to repent”—to turn away from a sinful course and return to obedience to God. In the New Testament, it is used both as a command and as a description of people who repented. Its emphasis is not merely feeling regret, but responding rightly to wrongdoing before God. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation, showing its repeated importance in calls to repentance and descriptions of those who responded. e.t: This word means “coin,” referring to a piece of money. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 22:19. That occurrence establishes its ordinary lexical sense, while the precise significance of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its actual wording. As a plain money term, it identifies something used in financial exchange.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “really.” It strengthens a statement by presenting something as genuine, actual, or certain rather than merely supposed. It functions as an adverb, helping emphasize the truth of what is being said. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, showing a recurring way to reinforce an assertion. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

e.t: This word means a crowd: a large gathering of people considered together. It is used throughout the Greek New Testament for groups who gather around Jesus, follow him, hear him teach, seek healing, or take part in public events. It can also describe a crowd involved in a wider scene, without stating that every person shares the same purpose or response. The word occurs 175 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that crowds are a recurring part of its narrative world.

e.t: This word means “rebellion”—a deliberate turning against rightful authority rather than simple weakness or confusion. It describes an act of resistance, and its meaning is plainly negative: the person or people involved refuse proper submission. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hebrews 3, where the surrounding passage supplies the fuller situation. Its precise force in either verse depends on that surrounding context, but the central idea remains rebellious opposition.

e.t: This verb means “to gain” or “to keep,” describing the obtaining or preserving of something. Its precise emphasis depends on the sentence: it may point to acquiring something or holding on to what has been obtained. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each in a different verse. The word therefore carries a practical sense of securing something, whether by gaining it or retaining it. Its basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent.

e.t: This word means “to foretell”: to announce something before it happens. It describes giving advance notice of what is to come, rather than merely speaking about an event after it has occurred. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Acts—Acts 3:18 and Acts 7:52. The word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains declaring beforehand what will happen.

e.t: This word means “to encourage”—to give someone support, confidence, or urging toward a course of action. It describes an act of strengthening another person rather than merely offering information. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 18:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a positive effort to hearten, assist, or urge someone onward.

d: Ptolemais, a coast city of Phoenicia, midway between Tyre and Caesarea.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine, Location

e.t: Ptolemais is a proper name identifying a place, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore primarily geographical: it names a location mentioned in the New Testament. The name occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 21:7. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word itself identifies the place but does not by itself explain the events or significance associated with it.

e.t: This word means “to leap” or describes something that “leaped,” expressing a sudden springing movement. It is used for physical movement rather than merely standing or walking. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Luke, and is rendered “leaped” or “leap.” Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a lively upward or forward movement.

d: To cut short, bring to swift accomplishment, determine, decide.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “shortly” or “to cut short.” It describes bringing something to a shorter duration or limiting its extent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 9:28, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its central idea remains clear: something is shortened, brought to a swift conclusion, or made brief. The surrounding verse determines exactly how that idea functions there.

d: Syria, a great Roman imperial province, united with Cilicia.

e.t: This word means “Syria,” the name of a geographical region. It functions as a place-name in the Greek New Testament, identifying a location rather than describing a person, action, or quality. The word occurs eight times in eight New Testament verses, especially in Acts, and is also found in Matthew, Luke, and Galatians. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means a wall or walls: a built structure that encloses, protects, separates, or forms part of a city or other place. In the Greek New Testament, it is a noun used for literal walls, including structures connected with escape, fortified cities, and the heavenly city described in Revelation. It occurs nine times in nine New Testament verses, with six occurrences in Revelation. The basic idea remains the same whether the word refers to one wall or multiple walls; the surrounding passage identifies the particular structure in view.

It points to a person marked by insolence rather than merely someone who makes a mistake or acts weakly. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Romans and once in 1 Timothy. Its exact force in either passage is understood more fully from the surrounding verse and passage.

Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains the action of putting on.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in Luke, Ephesians, James, and Revelation. Its basic idea remains elevation—being high, raised, or above a lower position. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and subject.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to need.” It describes a person’s lack of something necessary or the requirement for help, provision, or support. The word is used five times in the Greek New Testament, so it expresses a straightforward idea rather than a broad range of meanings. Its exact object—what is needed—comes from the surrounding sentence and passage. The same basic sense appears whether the need concerns daily provision, personal assistance, or credentials for ministry.

e.t: This word refers to a false Christ: someone presented as Christ or claiming Christ’s place without truly being him. It is plural in meaning when rendered “false Christs,” pointing to more than one such person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22. Those references identify the word’s setting, while the central meaning remains a counterfeit claimant to the title and identity of Christ.
